<reason>Side A built a stronger case by framing shared rent-setting tools as a hub-and-spoke coordination mechanism functionally equivalent to a consultant-led cartel, effectively countering Side B's agreement requirement argument with the point that delegation to a common agent constitutes agreement and that retained discretion to cheat does not negate conspiracy. A also exposed a fatal circularity in B's position: demanding proof of hidden coordination before scrutiny when the evidence sits inside the platform contracts. While B made valid points about categorical overbreadth and the legal distinction between parallelism and agreement, A successfully narrowed the motion to target private data pooling and distinguished scrutiny from liability, giving them the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.1-A4.5), particularly the argument that demanding proof of hidden data exchanges before scrutiny creates a circular trap where the most effective coordination faces the least examination, combined with the rebuttal that discretion to deviate does not negate agreement (as cartel members can also cheat).</best_rebuttal>
